Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I can't deal with even the slightest upset
The event happened because of the way I acted

vignette: Eleanor Vance was twenty-two when a man she briefly spoke to at a desert rest stop lured her onto a backroad and locked her in a subterranean room for twenty-one days. The air was thick and still. She learned the exact number of hairline cracks in the concrete ceiling, the rhythmic scrape of boots above, the way her own voice would dissolve into the damp silence. When she finally escaped, the quiet followed her home. In the weeks that followed, the past refused to settle. Eleanor found herself staring at her own bedroom ceiling, certain the stale air of that basement was bleeding through her walls. Her memories of those days did not blur or soften; they arrived in her mind with the sharp, unblinking clarity of photographs. She could count the rust stains on the sink, the precise angle of the single barred window, the way the weak light fell across the floorboards at exactly three in the afternoon. Yet when she tried to hold onto these images, a strange distance settled over her. The girl in those mental frames seemed to belong to a stranger. That was not her life, she would tell herself, even as the sensations rushed back. They felt more real than her own kitchen, more real than the faces of her friends. When the memories came, they did not wait for permission. They would surface suddenly, without warning, and hijack her attention mid-sentence during roll call or while she was coiling a hose, and suddenly she was standing in that room again, her hands gripping cold iron, her muscles pulling toward escape. She tried to move, to call out, until a dispatcher's voice cut through the haze and brought her back to the apparatus bay. Ordinary sounds became uninvited alarms. The heavy thud of her fire station locker shutting, the hiss of the coffee pot in the break room, even the distant whine of a garbage truck down the street would make her jump, her breath catching in her throat. She could not explain why her body would lock up at a dropped pen or a slamming car door, only that the reflex felt as urgent as it had in the dark. Even when she knew she was safe, she could not relax. Her shoulders stayed braced, her breathing shallow, as if waiting for the floor to give way. Alongside this erosion of self, even small frustrations accumulated into a suffocating certainty that she had no strength left to manage anything at all. She looked in the mirror and felt like a stranger wearing her face, unsure of who she was supposed to be outside the memory of those walls. And beneath it all, a quiet, persistent voice insisted that she had brought it on herself. She replayed the moments leading up to her capture, tracing every glance, every decision, convinced that if she had just acted differently, spoken differently, moved differently, she would not have ended up in that basement. Her life as a firefighter demanded a pace that left little room for stillness, and the culture of the station eventually forced a kind of retreat. She stopped going to the Sunday post-shift gatherings, citing overtime, because the noise and pressing bodies in the station's rec room made her chest tighten. She began leaving her locker at the far end of the gear bay and taking a different route to the shower room, avoiding the narrow corridors where she felt boxed in. When she found an old wallet photo from before the captivity-a smiling girl with her hair down-she slipped it into a shoebox at the back of her closet and told herself she would deal with it later, though she knew she would not open it. Now, at twenty-six, Eleanor sits in a therapist's office for the first time, her hands folded tightly in her lap. The decision to come here did not come from a single breaking point, but from the slow accumulation of a life shrinking around her. She no longer recognizes the woman who used to sleep through the night or laugh without bracing herself. What brings her to this chair is the dawning realization that she cannot keep outrunning the past, and the quiet, desperate hope that she might finally learn how to breathe again without flinching at the sound of her own heartbeat.
